openers.ordovician-period: In the Ordovician, the sea filled up. Marine animal life radiated through the period, and the Cambrian fauna gave way to one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. Nautiloids reached their peak variety, starfish and brittle stars appeared, and new reef builders brought reefs back after a long lull. The Iapetus Ocean, over 4,000 km wide at the start, began to narrow. The period opens with a single conodont species, Iapetognathus fluctivagus, appearing in the rock record.
openers.early-ordovician-epoch: The Early Ordovician was a time of rising water and new arrivals. Sea level climbed almost without pause, and shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana. Into them came phacopid trilobites, starfish, reef-building stromatoporoid sponges and strophomenid brachiopods. Several invertebrate lineages took to open water and started new food chains. Morocco's Fezouata Shale preserves the soft-bodied animals of this world, while trackways in Western Australia may record animals walking on land.
openers.middle-ordovician-epoch: The Middle Ordovician is when the climate turned. Oxygen isotopes in conodonts show the shift from greenhouse to icehouse beginning, and a long ice age followed. On land, the spores of the first plants appear about 470 million years ago, and atmospheric oxygen began a long rise. In space, the break-up of an asteroid sent fragments toward Earth, and craters from Iowa to Quebec date to this time. The first sea urchins appear in the seas below.

reviews.ordovician-period: The Ordovician turned a Cambrian sea into a Paleozoic one. Marine life radiated until diversity had risen severalfold, with nautiloids at their peak and suspension feeders and swimmers filling the water. Meanwhile the Iapetus Ocean narrowed, letting seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents. By the end of the period, the template for the rest of the Paleozoic seas was set.
reviews.early-ordovician-epoch: The Early Ordovician laid the foundations of the great radiation. Seas rose over the continents, and in those warm shallows new trilobites, echinoderms, brachiopods, sponges and corals appeared, with the first crinoids, eurypterids and horseshoe crabs. Plankton multiplied, feeding both seafloor filter feeders and swimmers. The climate was a super-greenhouse, yet animals thrived. Avalonia broke away and opened the Rheic Ocean, and the Taconic mountains began feeding nutrients to the sea.
reviews.middle-ordovician-epoch: The Middle Ordovician links cooling, plants and oxygen. As the climate shifted toward icehouse, biodiversity rose in step. The first land plants began burying organic carbon, drawing down CO2 and helping atmospheric oxygen rise. Impacts from a shattered asteroid struck at about a hundred times today's rate, and one crater at Decorah filled with exceptional fossils. By about 460 million years ago, glaciers were spreading on Gondwana, beginning the long Early Paleozoic Ice Age.

ordo-009.title: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event
ordo-009.text:
Global marine diversity rose severalfold in the Ordovician. Through the period, marine animal life radiated and replaced the Cambrian fauna with one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. The animal phyla filled out with many new classes and smaller groups. This was the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, or GOBE.

It was not one sudden burst. Different groups diversified at different times, from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician, and not everywhere at once.

What drove it is still argued. Proposed causes include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower. Whatever the mix, the outcome was lasting. The GOBE set the ecological template of the seas for the rest of the Paleozoic.

ordo-010.title: The Iapetus Ocean narrows
ordo-010.text:
At the start of the Ordovician, the Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide. It did not stay that way. Baltica drifted toward Laurentia, while island arcs and microcontinents such as Ganderia were added to Laurentia and Avalonia.

As the gap closed, animals responded. Seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents, while ostracods and fishes stayed isolated. Sources differ on the ending. Several say Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia had joined by the end of the Ordovician, forming Euramerica, also called Laurussia. Others place the final Laurentia–Baltica collision in the Silurian, during the Caledonian orogeny.

ordo-012.title: Nautiloids at their height
ordo-012.text: Straight, curved and coiled shells lived side by side in Ordovician seas, as nautiloids reached their peak variety. They spread from shallow waters into the open ocean at all latitudes. New orders such as Bisonocerida and Dissidocerida appear in the Early Ordovician, and Ascocerida early in the Middle Ordovician.

ordo-013.title: Green Point: where the Ordovician begins
ordo-013.text: One tiny tooth-bearing animal marks the start of a period. The Ordovician begins with the first appearance of the conodont Iapetognathus fluctivagus in the rock record. Its reference section, the GSSP, lies in the cliffs at Green Point in western Newfoundland, dated at 486.85 Ma. The period lasts about 43.75 million years, until the Silurian begins at 443.1 Ma. It is named after the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe of north Wales, where its rocks were first identified.

ordo-001.title: Rising seas drown the continents
ordo-001.text: Through the Early Ordovician, sea level rose more or less continuously, levelling off only around mid-period. Shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana. The flooding of Laurentia created warm shallows where shelled sea life thrived. North America's Transcontinental Arch, a ridge of high ground, went under water and would not reappear until the Devonian.

ordo-004.title: Phacopid trilobites and their crystal eyes
ordo-004.text: Trilobites with schizochroal eyes, built of separate, larger lenses, appear suddenly in the early Ordovician. The order Phacopida probably first appears then too; nine other trilobite orders had arisen in the Cambrian. During the Ordovician radiation, a new trilobite fauna replaced the old Cambrian one.

ordo-005.title: The first starfish and brittle stars
ordo-005.text: Starfish fall apart after death, which is why their fossil record is so sparse. The first true starfish lived in the Early Ordovician, alongside brittle stars, as echinoderm diversity rose and new classes appeared, among them the diploporitans. Paracrinoids appear in the Early Ordovician and cystoids in the Middle Ordovician.

ordo-006.title: Stromatoporoid sponges start building reefs
ordo-006.text: Stromatoporoids, extinct sea sponges that built reefs, first appear unambiguously in the Tremadocian, at the start of the Early Ordovician. Their reefs grew in South China from the start of the period and spread to North America and North China by mid-period. The first order, Labechiida, quickly spread worldwide in the Middle Ordovician and diversified abruptly in the mid-to-late Darriwilian.

ordo-007.title: The seas turn to calcite
ordo-007.text: The chemistry of seawater decides which minerals shells and cements form from. In the Cambrian, seas were mixed, precipitating both aragonite and calcite, two forms of calcium carbonate. By the early Ordovician they had given way to fully calcite seas, where calcite was the mineral that formed.

ordo-014.title: The Ordovician plankton revolution
ordo-014.text:
More plankton meant more of everything else. From the end of the Cambrian into the early Ordovician, several invertebrate lineages colonized open waters and started new food chains. This first phase of the GOBE, tied to plankton, ended in the late Early Ordovician.

Microscopic life boomed. Chitinozoans, flask-shaped microfossils, radiated explosively across the Tremadocian and later became key markers for dating rocks. Acritarchs, mostly marine algae, peaked in diversity and variety of form in the Middle Ordovician. With more food drifting overhead, suspension feeders on the seafloor and swimmers in the water column multiplied.

ordo-016.title: Reefs return after a Cambrian lull
ordo-016.text: Since the archaeocyath sponges died out, reefs had been rare. New reef-building corals changed that as they diversified in the Ordovician. Coral reefs emerged in the early Ordovician, including the earliest known octocorals, soft corals with eight-fold symmetry. By the middle Tremadocian, reefs of microbes and sponges occupied deeper water, as in South Korea's Dumugol Formation.

ordo-017.title: The Sauk Sea retreats from North America
ordo-017.text: At its peak, the shallow Sauk Sea had covered most of North America. Early in the Ordovician, a marine regression, a retreat of the sea, ended the Sauk sequence of rocks it had laid down. The Tippecanoe sequence followed later in the period, when the sea returned.

ordo-018.title: Strophomenid brachiopods spread across the shelves
ordo-018.text: Strophomenida, an order of articulate brachiopods, lived from the Early Ordovician to the mid Carboniferous. They were among the most diverse and abundant brachiopods of the Ordovician. Orthid brachiopods reached their peak diversity at the same time, in shallow-shelf seas. The Late Ordovician mass extinction hit the strophomenids hard.

ordo-019.title: Tumblagooda: footprints of uncertain age
ordo-019.text: Trackways in Western Australia's Tumblagooda Sandstone are read by some as the earliest evidence of animals living fully on land. Both that reading and the age are uncertain. Conodonts in overlying beds now point to an early Ordovician age, though a Silurian age was once favored. Because the unit is so poorly dated, it cannot show whether plants, which colonized land in the mid-Ordovician, got there first.

ordo-021.title: Fezouata: a Burgess Shale for the Ordovician
ordo-021.text: Aegirocassis, a filter-feeding arthropod over 2 m long, was the largest animal of its time, and it comes from Morocco's Fezouata Shale. This Early Ordovician site preserves exceptional soft-bodied fossils: over 1,500 specimens of 50 taxa. They resemble the Burgess Shale biotas of the Cambrian. That makes Fezouata a bridge between the Cambrian explosion and the GOBE, showing that soft-bodied communities carried on into the Ordovician.

ordo-022.title: Armored jawless fish with true bone
ordo-022.text:
The first vertebrates with true bone, jawless fishes, appear around 485 million years ago. Armored jawless fish called ostracoderms rose to prominence and remained the main vertebrates until the Devonian. Some accounts place the first small armored forms, such as a plated Laurentian group, already in the late Cambrian.

They stayed close to shore. Early fishes lived mainly in near-shore settings such as intertidal zones and shallow lagoons. The oldest named thelodonts, small fish covered in scales, Larolepis and Stroinolepis, come from the Late Ordovician Sandbian stage.

ordo-020.title: The Early Ordovician super-greenhouse
ordo-020.text: Sea surface temperatures may have reached 43.9 °C at 485 Ma. The Early Ordovician was very hot, comparable to the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, with very high carbon dioxide at the start of the period. One set of estimates shows the seas cooling to 37.1 °C by 470 Ma. The long-lasting heat shaped the biodiversification that followed in the Middle Ordovician.

ordo-024.title: Avalonia breaks free and opens the Rheic Ocean
ordo-024.text:
Pieces of future Newfoundland, southern Britain and New England once sat on the edge of Gondwana. Around 480 Ma they broke free as the microcontinent Avalonia. A rift between them grew into a mid-ocean ridge, opening the Rheic Ocean in the Early Ordovician.

As Avalonia drifted north, it closed the Iapetus Ocean ahead of it and opened the Rheic behind it. It was not alone. Ganderia probably separated from Gondwana near the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, and Carolina, Armorica and other terranes on Gondwana's northern margin also broke away during the Ordovician.

ordo-025.title: Damara thrusting comes to an end
ordo-025.text: Gondwana's last seam closed slowly. In the Damara orogeny, thrusting onto the Kalahari Craton continued until 480 Ma, long after the main collisions. The Damara–Kuunga orogeny was the final joining of northern and southern Gondwana, and with its end the supercontinent was complete.

ordo-026.title: The first crinoids, the sea lilies
ordo-026.text: The earliest unequivocal crinoids, or sea lilies, date to about 480 million years ago, in the middle Tremadocian. These stalked echinoderms, with feathery arms that catch food, went through the first of their two major adaptive radiations during the Ordovician. They became a lasting part of Paleozoic seafloors.

ordo-027.title: The first eurypterids, the sea scorpions
ordo-027.text: The earliest known eurypterids, or sea scorpions, date to the Tremadocian, about 480 million years ago. Several branches already existed by the Middle Ordovician, which suggests the group arose in the Cambrian. The first truly successful ones were the Laurentian megalograptids, which radiated in the Late Ordovician. Most groups appear in the Silurian.

ordo-028.title: The first horseshoe crabs
ordo-028.text: Horseshoe crabs, or xiphosurans, first appear in the Early Ordovician, around 480 million years ago. The oldest known specimens come from Morocco's Fezouata Formation and are still undescribed. The oldest named early relative, Lunataspis, lived in what is now Canada about 445 Ma.

ordo-029.title: Insects begin, by a molecular estimate
ordo-029.text: Insects are estimated to have originated about 480 million years ago, around when land plants appeared. The estimate comes from a 2014 study that compared genes, not from fossils. It allows an origin as early as the Early Ordovician or even the Cambrian. In this version, insects' early radiation happened no later than 479 Ma, in marine or coastal settings.

ordo-030.title: The Taconic orogeny raises the first Appalachians
ordo-030.text:
A great mountain chain once ran from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States. It rose when volcanic island arcs collided with Laurentia in the Taconic orogeny, the first Paleozoic mountain building in North America. A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician prepared the collision, and the orogeny affected most of New England.

The mountains reached far beyond themselves. Their erosion fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE. Later, the weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew down CO2 in the Late Ordovician.

ordo-031.title: From greenhouse to icehouse
ordo-031.text:
By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude sea surfaces had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures. Oxygen isotopes in conodont teeth show the shift from greenhouse to icehouse beginning at the end of the Early Ordovician. A sharp rise in carbon isotope ratios in the Floian may mark cooling through the burial of organic carbon, and it is proposed to have kick-started the GOBE.

Life and cold rose together. Biodiversity climbed in step with cooling during the GOBE. Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse state by about 460 million years ago.

ordo-033.title: The Decorah impact in Iowa
ordo-033.text: A meteor about 200 m wide struck what is now Decorah, Iowa, around 470 million years ago. It released energy equal to 1,000 megatons of TNT. The possible crater, about 5.6 km across, now lies buried under the Winneshiek Shale. It may be part of the Ordovician meteor event, a shower of impacts from a shattered asteroid.

ordo-034.title: The first land plants leave their spores
ordo-034.text:
The first land plants are known by their spores. Cryptospores appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossil assemblages for some 60 million years. The plants that made them evolved from green algae. The earliest were bryophytes, similar to mosses and liverworts.

Baltica was an early cradle. By the Darriwilian it already held a diverse flora.

Small as they were, these plants changed the planet. By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down CO2 and transforming both land environments and the global climate. There were limits to what they could do. Without deep roots, they did little to break rock into soil, a job left to the larger plants that came later.

ordo-032.title: Clearwater East: one crater, not a twin
ordo-032.text: Two craters sit side by side in Quebec, but they are not twins. The 26 km Clearwater East crater formed about 460–470 Ma, by argon-argon dating of its impact melt. Its neighbor, Clearwater West, formed much later, in the Early Permian, and the two carry different meteorite signatures. Clearwater East's central peak lies hidden under lake water and sediment; depth surveys and core drilling confirmed it.

ordo-035.title: The Paleozoic Oxidation Event begins
ordo-035.text: Between 470 and 400 Ma, oxygen in the air rose in what is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. The first land plants, spreading from about 470 to 445 Ma, helped drive it. They trapped organic carbon in sediments, where it could no longer react with oxygen, so less oxygen was used up. The rise kept going. Oxygen later reached and exceeded today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

ordo-037.title: The Ordovician meteor shower
ordo-037.text:
About 100 times as many meteorites struck Earth each year as today, and the raised rate lasted for millions of years. The cause lay in space: the break-up of the parent body of the L-chondrite meteorites sent fragments into orbits crossing Earth's.

The evidence still falls from the sky. Many L-chondrites that land today carry shock ages from the break-up, and helium-3 in seafloor sediments supports the event. Craters such as Ames, 16 km across in Oklahoma, Rock Elm, 6 km in Wisconsin, and Slate Islands, and possibly Decorah and Granby, may belong to this shower. It was once suggested to have sparked the GOBE, but other evidence puts it about 600,000 years after the Darriwilian diversity burst.

ordo-038.title: The first sea urchins
ordo-038.text: The earliest echinoid fossils, the first sea urchins, date to the Middle Ordovician, around 465 million years ago. They joined the growing list of echinoderm classes that appeared in the Ordovician. The shallow-water limestones of Estonia, from the Ordovician and Silurian, are famous for their echinoids.

ordo-041.title: The Winneshiek Shale fills an impact crater
ordo-041.text: An impact crater became a fossil trap. Sediments that filled the Decorah crater in Iowa preserve conodonts, bivalved arthropods and the earliest eurypterids in exceptional detail. The quiet, enclosed basin left by the impact kept these animals intact, giving a rare view of Ordovician life in about 460 million-year-old rock.

ordo-040.title: The Early Paleozoic Ice Age
ordo-040.text:
Ice spread over Gondwana while carbon dioxide was still high. A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago. Glaciers were probably present by the Sandbian, with several short glaciations then and in the Katian. In the Ordovician the ice centered on the Sahara; in the Silurian it shifted to South America. It is known from Arabia, West Africa and the Andes.

Geography may explain it. Gondwana sat over the South Pole, which may have let ice form despite the high CO2. As ice caps grew and melted, sea level rose and fell.
